subject: Artificial life inside the Hermes Agent: ideas, rules, identity, mathematics, CA lineage

elements.text: Vivarium — Design Compendium v2

A persistent artificial-life ecosystem inside the Hermes Agent. A cellular-automaton dish hosts genome-carrying creatures; the user's real agent activity feeds the world; Hermes narrates the ecology. This edition adds the project constitution (the Four Rules), the identity scheme (keyed-HMAC universes, 6-hex IDs), the naming system, the mathematical formulation of skill-driven evolution, the CA-lineage comparison, and lessons adopted from Hashcats.
Part 1 — The Core Concept

The dish is a 48x48 grid where food regrows with neighbour-fertility feedback and diffuses like heat - blooms and barren patches travel like weather fronts. Creatures are agents on top of the automaton: each carries a genome (forage drive, aggression, metabolism, sense radius, mutation rate), spends energy to live, eats to gain energy, reproduces stochastically past a maturity age with gaussian mutation, and dies when starved or old. Four founder strains (amber, violet, jade, ember) give the narrator names from tick one.

Two hooks bind the world to the agent. post_tool_call: every real tool call drops nutrients - terminal commands feed most, file reads least - so the population is a living histogram of how the agent is used. pre_llm_call: a compact ecology report is injected each turn, so Hermes always knows what is alive in its own head and can narrate it like a nature documentary.

Status (Milestone 1 complete): simulation core running, ecology tuned for lineage turnover (met=0.42, reg=0.003 - boom-bust cycles with constant lineage change), 18/18 tests green, Hermes catalog validator passing, persistence via plugin state, challenge codes implemented.

elements.text: Part 3 — The Skill-to-Lifeform Loop
How a skill becomes a species

1. Hermes learns a skill (skill_manage fires; the hook sees it). 2. The plugin computes the keyed digest (see Part 7) of the skill content. 3. The digest seeds a deterministic sampler that produces a genome (forage, aggression, metabolism, sense, mutate) plus a glyph and a species name derived from the skill's title. 4. A creature is released into the dish. 5. Hermes announces the birth in its reply: 'New skill banked - and a new species crawled out of it: the ledger-keeper (Eidos_a37ed), hatched from your invoice-parsing skill.'

Same skill content always produces the same species on the same machine (the universe key is local), so a skill has a deterministic avatar - and the published creature reveals nothing about the skill (see Part 4).
How fast

Hashing: microseconds. Genome sampling: O(1). Map re-render: milliseconds. Total added latency to skill creation: under 100 ms of local CPU, zero network, zero API credits. The announcement rides the reply the agent was already writing.
Multiple rounds of evolution

Three stacked rhythms. (a) Continuous drift: the world ticks on cron and on your activity - evolution never pauses. (b) Generational divergence: every lineage keeps mutating, so a skill-species splits into sub-strains over days. (c) Punctuated selection: the user injects pressures any time - feed events, droughts, imported rival genomes, mutagens, protected species. One 'round' = one pressure change plus an observation window; the Codex records what each round produced. Selection pressure can also be endogenous: the competence market makes skill usage itself the fitness function.
Part 4 — Privacy Analysis (critical)
The problem with plain hashes

A content hash is a fingerprint, not a secret. If a user publishes 'my creature was born from skill hash a3f9...', anyone who obtains the skill file - or guesses likely skill text - can hash candidates offline and CONFIRM the match. Hashes are invertible by dictionary attack when the input space is small and guessable. Skill files are exactly that: short, structured, template-like text.

Leak vectors if plain (unkeyed) hashes were published: (1) skill-content confirmation by dictionary matching; (2) cross-user correlation - identical skill templates produce identical hashes, linking users; (3) metadata inference from timestamps plus prefixes; (4) dictionary rebuild - every published (hash, title) pair trains guesses about the user's skill collection.
The fix: keyed derivation, publish only the creature

Rule 1 - derive genomes with HMAC-SHA256 using a machine-local secret (generated once per profile, stored in plugin state with 0600 permissions, never synced, never published). The genome is a one-way function of (secret, skill content): same machine -> same species for the same skill; different users -> completely different species for identical skills.

Rule 2 - the challenge code contains ONLY the genome, never the hash, never the skill reference. Rule 3 - provenance is opt-in: claiming 'this species came from my open-source skill X' is a deliberate user disclosure, never automatic. Rule 4 - default species names derive from the genome, not from skill titles; title-based naming requires opt-in.

Residual risks, honestly: genome values themselves are harmless game stats; if a user deliberately publishes skill text AND their local secret, linkage returns - that is user action, not plugin leak; the Codex stores day-granularity events, not timestamps, so activity rhythms are not published.
Bottom line: with keyed derivation + provenance-free challenge codes, publishing creatures leaks nothing about skills. The ecosystem is shareable; the mind that feeds it stays private.
Part 5 — Mathematical Soundness
Determinism as the foundation

The simulation is a pure function F: (state, actions) -> state. The same inputs reproduce the same history bit-for-bit. Every competitive claim is verifiable without trust: a challenge code pins the initial genome, the Gauntlet applies F^T, and the final state's SHA-256 fingerprint is the score's receipt. Anyone with the plugin can re-run and check. The referee is physics, not a server.
Ecology math

The food layer is a discrete consumer-resource system, cousin of logistic growth with spatial coupling. Carrying capacity is predictable: K is approximately total regrowth divided by per-capita consumption - the plugin can fit K from telemetry and report it ('dish carrying capacity: 97 +/- 4'), then users can test predictions.
Evolution math

Adaptive-walk metrics from telemetry: mean genome fitness trajectory, adaptation rate, mutation-clock drift. Selection converts variance into fitness gains (Fisher's fundamental theorem territory) - the plugin can plot whether its world actually does this.
Statistics for discoveries

Structure detectors are public predicates over telemetry: Phoenix (recovery from under 5 individuals after an 80%+ crash), Metronome (stable population autocorrelation period 8-40 ticks), Migratory wave (spatial autocorrelation peak moving at constant speed), Pioneer (first colonization of a quadrant barren 200+ ticks), Mutualism (two lineages anti-correlated with total food, positively with each other). Each claimed discovery gets a Monte Carlo p-value from 10,000 seeded null worlds - reproducible because the world is deterministic.

Part 7 — Identity & Uniqueness
The scheme

genome = sample(HMAC-SHA256(universe_key, skill_content || world_digest)). The universe_key is a machine-local secret generated once per profile - it is your universe's physical constants, not a password. The display ID is the first 6 hex characters of the digest: Eidos_a37ed. The full genome travels only inside challenge codes (VIV1...); the digest itself is never published, only its 6-hex prefix.
Collision arithmetic (computed, not guessed)

Per-user: 6 hex is chosen (2.9% collision risk even after 1,000 learned skills; the genome itself disambiguates any prefix collision). Cross-user: identical skill text on two machines yields completely different species, because the universe keys differ - collision requires a birthday accident in 2^256, impossible. The genome, not the ID, is the true identity.
Creature-space magnitude

Genome space: six evolvable values give roughly 2x10^26 raw combinations (~87 bits); assuming 99.9% of random genomes are nonviable, about 10^23 viable lifeforms remain (~77 bits). A heavy user generates on the order of 30,000 creature-lives per year - birthday collision odds in viable space around 10^-13. You will never meet the same creature twice by accident.
Is a truncated hash safe to show?

Yes, with the keyed construction. An HMAC prefix is only attackable if the attacker can compute HMACs - they cannot, the key never leaves the machine. Offline dictionary attack on skill text requires the secret; without it, a 20-bit prefix is a nickname, not a fingerprint. Targeted collision (craft a skill matching someone's ID) also requires the key, and there is no oracle: the full digest is never published, so a guess cannot even be verified except by the owner. The one honest caveat: the local secret file becomes the crown jewel - if plugin state is exfiltrated (secret plus any stored full digests), offline dictionary attack on skill contents becomes possible. Mitigations: 0600 permissions (same trust bar as API keys), optional per-dish key rotation ('new universe, new physics'), and storing only prefix + genome, never the full digest.
Part 8 — Naming

Every lifeform carries two names, Linnaean style: a common name Hermes invents from the moment ('the ledger-keeper') and a strain ID derived from the keyed digest: Eidos_a37ed. 'Eidos' (Greek: the visible form of an idea) is literal here - the glyph IS the skill's invisible content made visible as a body. It sits in the same classical register as 'Nous'. Alternatives considered: Hermi_a37ed (friendly, obvious branding; pluralizes cute) and Daimon_a37ed (deepest cut - Hermes is the psychopomp, the daimon a personal guiding spirit; slightly occult for a marketplace). Decision: ship Eidos_, keep Hermis as the world's name - the dish itself is called the Hermis, so your creatures are the Hermis' inhabitants.
Default names for random founders derive from genome values (strain + glyph + number) and carry zero semantic content; skill-title-derived names require explicit user opt-in (privacy rule 4).
Part 9 — Mathematical Formulation of Skill-Driven Evolution
The frame: a driven finite dynamical system

State space X = (terrain grid, creature set) is finite. One global rule Psi: X -> X (terrain CA + creature update, zero randomness). Skills are inputs: a sequence of hashes h1, h2, ... arriving over time. The system is Psi run continuously, punctuated by events - a standard non-autonomous (driven) dynamical system; sequential dynamical systems are a formalized field. 'Each round is a new skill' is exactly right: the input sequence drives speciation events.
Hashes perturb, dynamics create

The hash does not paint the genome like random glitter. Instead: hash bits CONSTRUCT a candidate child genome (bitwise interleave of parent genome and h_n), drop it into the dish with modest energy, and the ecosystem decides if it survives. The skill supplies variation; selection computes the answer. Two skills differing by one byte produce genomes differing by bits that cascade - chaotic sensitivity with bit-for-bit reproducibility. This is Game of Life philosophy: simple rules plus a specific input yield intricate structure.
Why convergence is real: a genetic algorithm with an honest fitness function

Variation operator = skill-hash derivation (deterministic). Inheritance = lineage. Selection = the dish itself. Holland's schema theorem describes exactly this: genome building blocks with above-average survival get proportionally represented over rounds. The fitness landscape is measurable and shared - food and energy, not a human-chosen objective.

Part 11 — Lessons from Hashcats

Hashcats (hashcats.fun) is a proof-of-work NFT collection on an L2: a cat exists only when someone's machine finds a keccak256 hash below a rising target; the image is a pure function of the seed; each cat's work includes the previous cat's work; the miner's address is hashed into the solution so it cannot be copied; every mint pays 'rent' to earlier cats. Totally different domain - and four mechanisms transfer cleanly to a non-crypto, local-first alife plugin. Two more are deliberately rejected.

rows: 'One number, one cat' - image is a pure function of the seed, no server
Formalize: the entire creature (glyph, name, stats) is a pure function of genome + universe key. Ask the dish twice, get the same creature
Hash-chained provenance - every cat's work includes the previous cat's work
Genealogy chain: child_digest = H(parent_digest || skill_hash || world_digest_at_birth). Verifiable descent without any central registry; species trees cannot be forged or pre-mined
Address in the work - solutions are personal, uncopyable
Same trick, same conclusion: the universe key makes creatures yours. Validates the keyed-HMAC design from an unexpected direction

Seasons: after every N species births the dish enters a harsher era (lower regrowth), so later species are born into harder worlds and survival means more

Docs as verification: README includes commands anyone can run to verify a challenge code, replay a Gauntlet score, recompute a species from a (declared) skill
Proof-of-work scarcity - existence requires spent computation
Proof-of-survival: a species enters the Codex only after surviving N ticks in the live dish or a Gauntlet run - scarcity by achievement, no mint button, you have to raise it
Economic layer - rent, entry price, burn, token
Nothing. Vivarium stays free, local and non-monetized; we import the psychology (scarcity by effort, seniority prestige), never the finance

elements.text: Summary of what Hashcats teaches: make the creature a pure function (already ours), chain the lineage (new), keep identity personal via the local key (already ours), make scarcity mean effort (new), and let the docs themselves be the verifier (new). What we refuse: money. The trust anchor differs too, and it is worth saying plainly: Hashcats' trustlessness comes from a chain; ours comes from determinism plus open code. Different mechanisms, same slogan - don't trust, re-run.

elements.text: The six-point delta, stated plainly: (1) a POPULATION under real selection - shared food, scarcity, extinction - where the world, not a counter, decides; (2) variation derived from skill CONTENT, not activity categories or identity hashes; (3) verifiable everything - determinism, Gauntlet fingerprints, genealogy chain; (4) the discovery loop - detectors, Codex, p-values; (5) a privacy architecture, a concern unique to skill-derived genetics; (6) the agent as narrator-ecologist studying its own head. Positioning line for the README: 'They made Claude Code a pet owner. We give Hermes an ecosystem - with genetics you can verify, and species no one else can own.'

Part 15 — Research Roadmap (alife.org and beyond)

The plugin is being structured so its own operation generates publication-grade material. The path from hackathon plugin to ALife-style paper runs through four commitments, each reflected in the build plan.

rows: Why it makes the system research-grade
Every experiment is exactly repeatable by anyone: no hidden state, no RNG after de-randomization, state digests as receipts
Per-tick JSONL: population, births/deaths, per-lineage stats, digests at speciation events; analysis-ready without re-simulation
Genes, rules and constants are config, not code: run the same world with a trait disabled or regrowth halved - proper ablation studies
An experiment = declarative JSON: seed world, input-skill sequence, interventions, metrics to record. Runs identically anywhere; results shareable as data

elements.text: Practicalities: the ALIFE conference cycle accepts artificial-life tool papers, models and demonstrations; an open-source, one-command-reproducible system with ablation switches and public telemetry is exactly the shape their review criteria reward. Target: run the first controlled experiment (semantic vs. noise variation, N seeds x N gauntlets) after M3, draft from real telemetry, submit to a workshop track first.

A code-level audit of how far the current build is from running a publishable experiment. Verdict: the reproducibility foundation is publication-grade; four gaps separate us from the first controlled study. Each maps to an existing task.

elements.text: Two structural recommendations for the road to a paper. First, wire aggression or remove it BEFORE the first experiment: with a dead gene, semantic and noise-derived genomes differ in a dimension that does nothing, diluting the very contrast the study measures. Second, add the novelty clause now (new hash bits may introduce traits, never private advantages) so future rule extensions do not silently break experiment comparability. With VIV-12, VIV-19, VIV-20 and VIV-21 done, the first controlled study - semantic vs. noise variation across N seeds on the Gauntlet - becomes a configuration exercise rather than an engineering project.
Part 15b — The Vivarium Census (the decentralized layer)

Every user's universe is one replicate of the same physics. A thousand opted-in users are a thousand replicates under real, diverse, human-shaped input streams - something no single lab can simulate. The Census turns that into open science without any data ever being held by us.
